title: How Many Different Numbers Are in a Range?

concept.title: Sort the questions by their right end; keep a 1 only at the latest occurrence of every value so far
body: A list of numbers and many questions are given. Each question gives a range `l..r` and asks for the **number of different values** in it. For `1 2 1 3 2` the range 1..3 has 2 different values (1 and 2) and the range 2..5 has 3 (2, 1 and 3). Counting each range with a set costs O(n) per question.

Answer the questions **offline**, in the order of their right ends. Walk a pointer `p` from 1 to `n`, and keep in a Fenwick tree a **1 at the position of the latest occurrence of every value seen so far** (and 0 elsewhere). When the value `a[p]` appears again, move its mark: add `-1` at its previous position and `+1` at `p`. Now, for a question whose right end is `p`, every different value in `[l, p]` is represented by exactly one mark in `[l, p]` (the last occurrence of that value not after `p`). So the answer is the number of marks in `[l, p]`, a range sum of the tree.

body.code:
order = sorted(range(q), key=lambda i: queries[i][1])    # by the right end
last = {}
t = [0] * (n + 1)
p = 0
for idx in order:
    l, r = queries[idx]
    while p < r:
        p += 1
        v = a[p - 1]
        if v in last: add(t, last[v], -1)       # the old mark moves
        last[v] = p; add(t, p, 1)
    answer[idx] = prefix(t, r) - prefix(t, l - 1)

body: The answers are stored by the original index of the question, so they are printed in the order of the input. Each position is processed once and each question costs two prefix sums: O((n + q) log n). The same idea ("keep only the last occurrence") counts distinct values in ranges, finds the mex of ranges and handles queries on colours.

statement: A list of `n` numbers and `q` questions are given. For every question `l r` print the number of different values among the positions `l` to `r`. Print the answers on one line, in the order of the questions.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `q`: the number of values and the number of questions.
Each of the next `q` lines has two numbers `l` and `r`: the question asks for the number of different values among the positions `l` to `r`.

examples.note: The ranges 1..3, 2..5 and 1..5 have 2, 3 and 3 different values.

hints: Answer the questions in increasing order of the right end.
Keep a mark only at the last occurrence of each value.
The answer is the number of marks in [l, r].

explanation: The questions are sorted by right end; a Fenwick tree holds a 1 at the latest occurrence of every value seen so far, and the answer to a question is the number of marks in its range.
solution.complexity: Time O((n + q) log n), space O(n + q).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

def bit_add(t, i, x):
    n = len(t) - 1
    while i <= n:
        t[i] += x
        i += i & -i

def bit_sum(t, i):
    s = 0
    while i > 0:
        s += t[i]
        i -= i & -i
    return s

n, q = map(int, input().split())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
qs = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(q)]

order = sorted(range(q), key=lambda i: qs[i][1])
last = {}
t = [0] * (n + 1)
p = 0
ans = [0] * q
for idx in order:
    l, rr = qs[idx]
    while p < rr:
        p += 1
        v = a[p - 1]
        if v in last:
            bit_add(t, last[v], -1)
        last[v] = p
        bit_add(t, p, 1)
    ans[idx] = bit_sum(t, rr) - bit_sum(t, l - 1)
print(*ans)
